articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.

This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran, though specific details of the changes were not immediately released. General Licenses typically permit certain categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, aiming to facilitate humanitarian aid, personal remittances, or other specific activities.

The issuance reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy towards Iran, which frequently involves a complex interplay of restrictions and authorizations to achieve foreign policy objectives while mitigating unintended consequences.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

These designations aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses associated with these regions. While specific details of the designated parties were not immediately available, such actions typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting transactions with the designated individuals and entities.
The move underscores the U.S. government's continued commitment to addressing threats posed by North Korea's weapons programs and instability in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, providing updated guidance on blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments are crucial for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations, as they clarify compliance obligations and best practices for handling transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.
The updated FAQs aim to enhance understanding and adherence to sanctions requirements, helping to prevent violations and ensure the effectiveness of U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 21, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, the removal of certain entities from Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists, and the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses.

The Iran-related designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities, while the removals from the Belarus and North Korea lists indicate specific policy adjustments. The new General Licenses for Iran and Russia aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, potentially easing some restrictions for specific sectors or activities.
These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, balancing pressure on adversarial regimes with efforts to mitigate humanitarian impacts or facilitate legitimate commerce where appropriate.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, alongside the issuance of associated General Licenses.

These designations target individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property, a critical area of national security and economic concern. The accompanying General Licenses are intended to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that might otherwise be impacted by these new designations.
This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American innovation and technology from foreign adversaries and illicit actors.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026.

This amendment and clarification aim to provide updated guidance on permissible activities involving Venezuela, potentially impacting various sectors such as oil, gas, and mining. General Licenses for Venezuela have been subject to frequent adjustments, reflecting the evolving U.S. policy towards the country.
The updated guidance is crucial for businesses and individuals engaged in Venezuela-related transactions to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026, along with the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations targeted 16 individuals and 10 entities for their roles in Iran's international financial networks and shadow banking activities, under Executive Order 13902 as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.' The Cuba designation further tightens restrictions on the Cuban regime.

The accompanying General Licenses and FAQs aim to clarify the scope of permissible activities under these updated sanctions regimes, which include authorizations for qualifying wind-down transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance through October 30, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026.

This action indicates a de-listing of an individual or entity from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Venezuela sanctions program. Such removals can occur due to various factors, including a change in circumstances, a successful petition for de-listing, or diplomatic considerations.
The removal of Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from the SDN List suggests a potential shift in specific aspects of the U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026.

These designations target individuals and entities involved in international narcotics trafficking and terrorism financing, aiming to disrupt their networks and limit their access to the U.S. financial system. Such actions are a critical component of the U.S. government's efforts to combat global illicit activities.
The designations underscore the ongoing commitment to protecting national security and preventing the flow of funds to criminal and terrorist organizations worldwide.

articles.headline: ECB Holds Rates Steady Amidst Rising Energy Inflation, Fed Also Pauses
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) held its key interest rates steady on October 29, 2026, with the deposit rate remaining at 2.50%, the main refinancing operations rate at 2.65%, and the marginal lending facility rate at 2.90%. This decision comes as euro-area inflation rose to 3.8% in September, primarily driven by a significant jump in energy inflation to 18.9%.

ECB President Christine Lagarde attributed the rise in inflation almost entirely to energy prices, citing a combination of oil, petrol, fuel, gas, and refining margins. She also noted that financing conditions have tightened, with 10-year sovereign yields increasing by approximately 35 basis points since September.

The ECB's decision follows a similar move by the U.S. Federal Reserve, which held its federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4% a day earlier. Both central banks are signaling that while they have paused rate hikes for now, they are not finished with their efforts to combat inflation, especially with persistent energy price volatility and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Ukraine.

articles.headline: Humanitarian Crises Deepen Across Middle East with Mass Displacement and Food Insecurity
body: Humanitarian crises are intensifying across the Middle East, with significant displacement and food insecurity reported in Lebanon, Gaza, and Yemen. In Lebanon, over 300,000 people remain internally displaced since early March, with the humanitarian situation described as 'far from over' by the UN's aid coordination office (OCHA).

In Gaza, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) warned of a deepening displacement 'nightmare,' as Israeli forces continue to push Palestinians into increasingly smaller areas while destroying civilian infrastructure and attacking displacement sites. Concerns of ethnic cleansing were also raised.

Yemen's conflict has displaced over 280,000 people, with many vulnerable individuals unable to access life-saving relief due to dangerous conditions. These ongoing crises underscore the urgent need for international intervention and humanitarian assistance to address the escalating suffering in the region.

articles.headline: OCC Releases October 2026 Bank Enforcement Actions, Including $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its monthly enforcement action report for October 2026, detailing various supervisory actions against OCC-supervised institutions. A significant action includes a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

The OCC also issued a cease and desist order and civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, for deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations, with an assessed civil money penalty of $350 million.

Additionally, the OCC issued Orders of Prohibition against several institution-affiliated parties, including Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds. These actions underscore the OCC's continued focus on AML/BSA compliance and individual accountability within financial institutions.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

articles.headline: DHS Adds Chinese Genomics Companies to UFLPA Entity List Over Forced Labor Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced additions to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List, effective October 29, 2026, targeting Chinese genomics companies. These additions include BGI Genomics Co., Ltd. (BGI Genomics), MGI Tech Co., Ltd. (MGI), and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co., Ltd. (BGI Group; BGI Holdings).

These entities are identified for working with the government of Xinjiang to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor or members of persecuted groups out of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR), or for sourcing material from Xinjiang or from persons working with the government of Xinjiang for forced labor programs. U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will apply a rebuttable presumption that goods produced by these entities are prohibited from entering the United States.

This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating forced labor in global supply chains and preventing goods made with forced labor from entering the U.S. market. The UFLPA Entity List now includes 190 entities, reflecting ongoing efforts to address human rights abuses in Xinjiang.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Homeland Security

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
